text: 115 Guidance for national tuberculosis programmes on the management of tuberculosis in children Annex 3 Administering, reading and interpreting a tuberculin skin test This annex gives information on administering, reading and interpreting a tuberculin skin test (TST). A TST is the intradermal injection of a combination of mycobacterial antigens that elicit an immune response (delayed-type hypersensitivity), represented by induration, which can be measured in millimetres. The standard method of identifying people infected with M. tuberculosis is the TST using the Mantoux method. Multiple puncture tests should not be used as these tests are unreliable (because the amount of tuberculin injected intradermally cannot be precisely controlled). This annex describes how to administer, read and interpret a TST using 5 tuberculin units (TU) of tuberculin PPD-S. An alternative to 5 TU of tuberculin PPD-S is 2 TU of tuberculin PPD RT 23. Administration 1. Locate and clean injection site 5–10 cm (2–4 inches) below elbow joint l Place forearm palm-up on a firm, well-lit surface. l Select an area free of barriers (e.g. scars, sores, veins) to placing and reading. l Clean the area with an alcohol swab. 2. Prepare syringe l Check expiry date on vial and ensure vial contains tuberculin PPD-S (5 TU/0.1 ml). l Use a single-dose tuberculin syringe with a short (¼- to ½-inch) 27-gauge needle with a short bevel. l Clean the top of the vial with a sterile swab. l Fill the syringe with 0.1 ml tuberculin. 3. Inject tuberculin (see Figure A3.1) l Insert the needle slowly, bevel up, at an angle of 5–15°. l Needle bevel should be visible just below skin surface. 4. Check injection site l After injection, a flat intradermal wheal of 8–10 mm diameter should appear. If not, repeat the injection at a site at least 5 cm (2 inches) away from the original site.
